Most of the people who give up are not defeated. They are early.

points.title: Comfort comes from a promise, not from circumstances.
points.body:
Psalm 119:50 says “My comfort in my suffering is this: Your promise preserves my life.”

Look where the comfort is located. Not in the suffering ending. Not in circumstances improving. In a promise — something said, that he decided to keep believing when nothing around him confirmed it.

That is a very specific spiritual skill, and it can be practised. It is the difference between “I feel better because things are better” and “I can keep going because God said something and God does not lie.”

supporting.text: My comfort in my suffering is this: Your promise preserves my life.

19.illustration:
When the civil war ended in January 1970, people who had held Biafran currency and brought it in to be exchanged were given a flat payment of twenty pounds, regardless of the amount they tendered.

Twenty pounds. Chinua Achebe put it into a short story called Civil Peace, where the character calls it the “egg-rasher” — a corruption of ex gratia. It has never left the Nigerian memory.

And what happened next is one of the most remarkable stories of recovery anywhere in the twentieth century.

Now — one correction, because I want you to hear this properly. Onitsha and Aba did not become trading cities after the war. They already were. Aba was a British military post from 1901, on the railway to Port Harcourt from 1915, and an industrial town by the 1930s. Onitsha’s market was famous enough in the 1950s to give its name to an entire literary genre — “Onitsha Market Literature.” Onitsha Main Market was destroyed in 1968.

So the story is not founding. It is re-building — which is harder, because you know exactly what you have lost.

They rebuilt it bigger. Onitsha Main Market is widely described as the largest market in West Africa. Ariaria International Market in Aba, established in 1976–77 after a fire destroyed the old Ekeoha Market, now has more than 37,000 stalls across three local government areas, serving Cameroon, Gabon and Central Africa, and known for its shoemaking as “the China of Africa.”

That took a generation. It also took the apprenticeship system we looked at on Day 4 — one man settling the next, over and over, for fifty years.
19.challenge:
Find one promise of God in Scripture that speaks to the exact thing you are currently enduring. Write it on paper. Put it somewhere you will see it every day for the rest of October.

Not a feeling. A promise. Psalm 119:50 in practice.
19.prayer: “Lord, when I am struck down, remind me I am not destroyed. Give me strength for the next step, not the whole road. Amen.”
19.code: The harvest is certain. The timing is not.

quiz.q: What flat payment were people given for surrendered Biafran currency when the war ended?
What did Chinua Achebe call the payment in his short story Civil Peace?
Which market was destroyed in 1968?

20.title: Shot on a Camcorder

scripture.text: We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not abandoned; struck down, but not destroyed.

20.truth: Build with what is in the warehouse, and let affliction teach what comfort cannot.
20.hook:
In 1992, a Lagos trader had a warehouse full of blank VHS tapes he could not sell.

So he decided to put something on them.

points.title: Build with what is in the warehouse.
points.body:
Nobody gave Kenneth Nnebue a film industry. He had blank tapes, a camcorder, actors nobody had heard of, and a country with no distribution system. He did not wait for conditions to improve. He built with what was in the room.

Nigerians are extraordinary at this. We call it “managing,” usually with a shrug, as if it were a failure. It isn’t. It is a national gift. The failure is when we use it as an excuse never to build the proper thing — Day 9’s lesson. But as a starting move? Building with what is in the warehouse is exactly right.

2 Corinthians 4:8–9 is four pairs, and every single one has a “but” in the middle. Hard pressed but not crushed. Perplexed but not in despair. Struck down but not destroyed. Paul is not denying the first half of any pair. He is refusing to let it be the last word.

points.title: Affliction is a teacher you would never have hired.
points.body:
Psalm 119:71 is an outrageous verse: “It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees.”

He is not saying the affliction was good. He is saying something was learned in it that would not have been learned anywhere else.

Nollywood learned things in its poverty that a well-funded industry never learns: how to shoot fast, how to distribute without a distributor, how to make a story carry a film when you cannot afford spectacle. Those constraints became competences.

Look at your own constraint — the money you do not have, the platform you were not given, the door that stayed shut. Ask the Psalm 119:71 question: what is this teaching me that comfort could not? Not “why me.” What is this teaching me?

supporting.text: It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees.

20.illustration:
Kenneth Nnebue was a trader. Celluloid film — real cinema — was financially out of reach for a Nigerian in 1992. So Living in Bondage was shot on a VHS camcorder, in Igbo with English subtitles, and sold direct to video.

He hired a director named Chris Obi Rapu — who worked under the fake name “Vic Mordi”, his wife’s maiden name, because he was Controller of Programmes at NTA at the time and was not allowed to freelance. Rapu has said he was paid ₦10,000 to direct it.

It reportedly sold over half a million copies within weeks.

Now, a correction, because Nigerians argue about this one publicly and you do not want to be on the wrong side of it. Living in Bondage did not birth Nollywood. Hubert Ogunde was making Nigerian films before it. Baba Sala. The Yoruba travelling theatre tradition. The Yoruba home-video pioneer Alade Aromire was working from around 1982. And Kenneth Nnebue himself had already produced a Yoruba-language home video before Living in Bondage.

Here is the accurate version, and it is still a great story: Living in Bondage was the breakout hit that proved the direct-to-video model could make serious money — and that is what industrialised Nollywood.

And the scale now: Nigeria’s own National Bureau of Statistics recorded 2,599 Nollywood films in 2020, up from 700 in 2019. On 2023 figures the motion picture, sound recording and music sector was ₦1.62 trillion of Nigerian GDP.

Twenty-seven years later, in November 2019, Ramsey Nouah directed a sequel — Living in Bondage: Breaking Free — which grossed ₦168.7 million at Nigerian cinemas. Cinemas that did not exist in any meaningful way when the first one was made.
20.challenge:
Name the resource you keep saying you need before you can start.

Now start a smaller version, today, without it. Not the whole plan. The version that fits in the warehouse.
20.prayer: “Lord, let me build in spite of my conditions, not wait for my conditions to improve. And teach me the things only hard seasons can teach. Amen.”
20.code: Build with what is in the warehouse.

quiz.q: In what year was Living in Bondage made and sold?
What language was Living in Bondage made in, with English subtitles?
Who directed the sequel, Living in Bondage: Breaking Free?

21.title: Three Naira to Nine

scripture.text: Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance.

21.truth: Trials produce something; they do not merely test something.
21.hook: At the Paris Olympics in 2024, Nigeria sent 88 athletes and won zero medals. At the Paris Paralympics, weeks later, Nigeria won seven and got a third of the money. Nobody threw them a parade.

points.title: Truth One: Trials produce something. They do not merely test something.
points.body: James does not say trials reveal your faith. He says the testing of your faith produces perseverance. It manufactures something that was not there before. And notice that he does not ask you to pretend it is pleasant. Consider it pure joy is a decision about how to regard the trial, not a claim about how it feels. Nobody enjoys the trial. James asks you to reckon it as gain because of what it is making.

points.title: Truth Two: Two true things at once.
points.body: Psalm 119:143 is one of the most emotionally accurate verses in Scripture: Trouble and distress have come upon me, but your commands give me delight. Both. At the same time. He does not say the trouble left. He does not say the delight replaced it. He holds both. That is what perseverance actually feels like from the inside. Not the absence of pain, but joy that survives alongside it. If you are waiting to feel fine before you decide you are persevering, you will wait forever.

points.title: One warning
points.body: Do not let this become they succeed because they are neglected. They succeed despite it, and the neglect has real costs, athletes going home with nothing. Admiring resilience must never become an excuse for the conditions that made resilience necessary. Celebrate the athletes. Then fix the budget.

supporting.text: Trouble and distress have come upon me, but your commands give me delight.

21.illustration: Here is the comparison. Total medals, all time: Paralympics 87 (40 gold), Olympics 27 (3 gold). All-time rank: Paralympics 37th, Olympics 80th. Tokyo 2020: Paralympics 10 medals, Olympics 2. Paris 2024: Paralympics 7 medals, Olympics 0. Nigeria first competed at the Paralympics at Barcelona in 1992, with six male athletes and three golds, and has competed at every Games since. Fifty-eight of those 87 medals are in athletics; most of the rest are in powerlifting, and overwhelmingly by women. Let me name one. Lucy Ejike. Powerlifter. Six Paralympic Games. Silver in Sydney 2000. Gold in Athens 2004, breaking the world record twice in one competition. Gold in Beijing 2008, world records on her first and second attempts. Silver in London 2012. Gold in Rio 2016, where she set three world records in a single competition, 135kg, then 138kg, then 142kg, and carried Nigeria's flag at the opening ceremony. Bronze in Tokyo 2020. Twenty-one years. Six Games. Six medals. And the money. For Paris 2024, the Federal Government allocated roughly ₦12 billion across both teams: reportedly ₦9 billion for the Olympic contingent and ₦3 billion for the Paralympic team. Three naira for every nine. The team that got nine came home with nothing. The team that got three came home with seven medals. And para-athletes who did not medal reportedly received no compensation at all from the Ministry of Sports, while team officials each received a thousand US dollars.
21.challenge: Find one person or group near you who is doing excellent work with almost no support, a school, a team, a small ministry, a carer. Do one concrete thing for them this week, and tell somebody else about them. Half of neglect is simply invisibility.
21.prayer: Lord, let my trials produce perseverance in me, not an excuse to quit. And open my eyes to the people around me doing great work that nobody is funding. Amen.

quiz.q: How many medals did Nigeria win at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
How many medals did Nigeria win at the Paris 2024 Paralympics?
How many Paralympic Games has Lucy Ejike competed in?

22.title: The Market That Burned

scripture.text: though he may stumble, he will not fall, for the LORD upholds him with his hand.

22.truth: Stumbling is not falling, because the question is whose hand is under you.
22.hook: On a Sunday in February 2023, the biggest market in Maiduguri burned down. Maiduguri, a city that had already absorbed more than a decade of insurgency, and hundreds of thousands of displaced people. And then the market, the engine of the whole city's economy, went up in flames. Eight months later it reopened.

points.title: Truth One: Stumbling is not falling.
points.body: Psalm 37:24 does not promise the righteous will never stumble. Read it again: though he may stumble. The stumble is assumed. What is promised is that it will not be the final word, for the Lord upholds him with his hand. There is a difference between a setback and an identity. The traders of Monday Market lost a market. They did not become people who used to trade. Whatever went wrong in your life this year, the business, the exam, the marriage, the health, the question is not whether you stumbled. You did. The question is whose hand is under you.

points.title: Truth Two: Weary with sorrow is not a lack of faith.
points.body: Psalm 119:28 is the most emotionally honest verse in this entire series: My soul is weary with sorrow; strengthen me according to your word. He does not open with praise. He does not perform. He says: I am exhausted and sad. And then he asks for strength. The psalmist names the weariness out loud to God, and that naming is where the request for strength begins. If you are tired today: you are not backslidden. You are at verse 28. Ask for the strength from where you actually are.

supporting.text: My soul is weary with sorrow; strengthen me according to your word.

22.illustration: Maiduguri's Monday Market burned on Sunday 26 February 2023. Thousands of traders lost everything in a night. The rebuilding was not a spontaneous act of self-reliance, and I am not going to pretend it was. Borno State released ₦2 billion to a rebuilding committee, plus ₦1 billion in disaster relief. Governor Babagana Zulum reopened the market in October 2023. Over eight thousand traders were allocated shops with two years' rent waived, and ₦800 million was distributed to 2,825 traders who could not be accommodated. Traders who had lost everything went back and started again, with a state that, in this instance, showed up and paid. Now, honesty, because this region deserves it. The wider story of return in Nigeria's north-east is not a happy one. Camps in Maiduguri were closed and food assistance stopped; between May 2021 and August 2022, Human Rights Watch documented over 140,000 people compelled to leave eight camps. People were resettled into places without healthcare, schooling or sanitation. And the security picture has deteriorated badly. In September 2025, an attack on Darul Jamal in Bama local government killed at least sixty people, who HRW records had returned from camps closed by the authorities a month earlier. So do not let anyone tell you the north-east is a finished story of triumph. It is an unfinished story of people getting up again in a place where getting up is still dangerous.
22.challenge: Say the true thing to God today, out loud if you can. Not the polished version. I am weary with sorrow. Then ask, in the same breath, for strength according to His word. That is a complete prayer and it is in the Bible.
22.prayer: Lord, uphold me when I stumble, so that stumbling is never mistaken for falling. My soul is weary, strengthen me according to Your word. Amen.

quiz.q: When did the Maiduguri Monday Market burn?
When did Governor Zulum reopen the market?
What does Psalm 37:24 say about the one who stumbles?
options: Though he may stumble, he will not fall
They will stumble and stay down

23.title: The Letter Nobody Acted On

scripture.text: Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall.

23.truth: Pride stops hearing, and humility often arrives through consequence, so pay attention to the small corrections.
23.hook: Twenty-one months before a building in Lagos collapsed and killed forty-four people, an engineering firm put its concerns in writing and walked away from the job. The letter exists. It is dated. The work continued anyway.

points.title: Truth One: Pride is not loudness. It is deafness.
points.body: We picture the proud man boasting. Proverbs 16:18 describes something quieter and far more dangerous: Pride goes before destruction. Before. It is a predictor. Why? Because pride removes your ability to see the fall coming. It does not shout. It just stops hearing. It reclassifies the engineer's letter as pessimism. It reclassifies the person who disagrees as not a team player. It reclassifies the regulator as an obstacle. And by the time the correction arrives, it is no longer a letter. It is a building. Ask yourself the only useful question here: when was the last time somebody told me something I did not want to hear, and I actually changed what I was doing? If you cannot remember, that is your answer.

points.title: Truth Two: Sometimes humility only arrives through consequence, and that is a mercy, not a punishment.
points.body: Psalm 119:67 is one of the most disarming admissions in the Psalms: Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I obey your word. He is not proud of that. He is simply telling the truth: he did not learn it the easy way. The correction had to cost him something before he took it seriously. Most of us are like that. So the small painful corrections in your life right now, the failure, the rebuke, the loss, the thing that humbled you in front of people, may be the cheapest lesson you will ever be offered. Pay attention to the cheap corrections, so that you never need the expensive ones. Forty-four people paid the expensive one.

supporting.text: Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I obey your word.

23.illustration: On 1 November 2021, at about a quarter to three in the afternoon, a twenty-one storey building under construction on Gerrard Road, Ikoyi, Lagos, collapsed. Forty-four people died, the toll rising from 42 in the first days of the search to 44 by 8 to 9 November, including the developer himself, Femi Osibona of Fourscore Heights Limited. His body was recovered on 4 November. Here is what came out afterwards. In February 2020, twenty-one months before the collapse, Prowess Engineering Limited withdrew from the project. Its Managing Director, Muritala Olawale, wrote to the owner limiting the firm's guarantee to the first two buildings and to work done up to the fourth floor of the third building, and citing the owner's failure to provide concrete cube tests at each stage. Concrete cube tests. That is the routine procedure where you take a sample of the concrete you are pouring and crush it, to confirm it is as strong as the design assumes. The firm withdrew. The work continued. And the Lagos State Building Control Agency had approved fifteen floors. Twenty-one were built. A Special Investigations Panel chaired by Toyin Ayinde reported on 5 January 2022. Lagos State accepted 26 of its 28 recommendations, ordered the demolition of the remaining towers, directed the prosecution of Fourscore Heights and the forfeiture of the site, and directed the prosecution of three town planners and civil servants for lying under oath and producing fake approvals through a private consulting company. Forty-four people. One letter. Twenty-one months.
23.challenge: Go to one person who has the standing to tell you the truth, a spouse, a colleague, a mentor, an older sibling, and ask them directly: What is the thing about my work, or my character, that you have been reluctant to tell me? Then say nothing except thank you. Do not defend. Do not explain. That is the whole exercise.
23.prayer: Lord, keep me correctable. Let me never mistake my position for permission to stop listening. And let me learn from the small corrections so I never need the large ones. Amen.
23.code: Pay attention to the cheap corrections

quiz.q: When did the Ikoyi building collapse?
How many people died in the collapse?
How many floors had the Lagos State Building Control Agency approved?

24.title: The Head of State Who Went Back to School

scripture.text: But he gives us more grace. That is why Scripture says: God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble.

24.truth: Humility is hardest in victory and most revealing in loss, and you are never finished learning.
24.hook: There is a document in a British university archive that I think is one of the most extraordinary things any Nigerian has ever produced. It is a PhD thesis. It was submitted by a man who, nine years earlier, had been the Head of State of Nigeria.

points.title: Truth One: Humility is hardest in victory, and most revealing in loss.
points.body: James 4:6 says God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble. Opposes is a strong word. It does not say God is disappointed by the proud. It says He sets Himself against them. Notice the two moments in Gowon's life where humility was tested, because they are opposite tests. In 1970 he had won, and he chose the language of reconciliation over triumph. In 1975 he had lost everything, and he chose to sit in a classroom rather than plot a return. Most of us can manage one of those. The person who does both has something real.

points.title: Truth Two: You are never finished learning, and status is the enemy of that.
points.body: The highest office he ever held did not persuade him he had nothing left to learn. Nigeria has a deep problem with this. We treat a title as a terminal qualification. Once you are Chief, once you are Doctor, once you are Pastor, once you are Oga, the learning is supposed to be over, and being corrected becomes an insult. Psalm 119:75 goes even further: I know, Lord, that your laws are righteous, and that in faithfulness you have afflicted me. He receives the hard thing as an act of God's faithfulness, not as evidence of God's absence. That is an extremely mature posture and it does not come cheaply. But it is available. It is the difference between a setback that teaches you and a setback that only embitters you.

supporting.text: I know, Lord, that your laws are righteous, and that in faithfulness you have afflicted me.

24.illustration: We met General Yakubu Gowon on Day 11, at the end of the civil war, saying no victor, no vanquished, and we were honest about the fact that the follow-through is still argued about. Today, the second half of his life. On 29 July 1975, while he was attending an OAU summit in Kampala, Uganda, Gowon was overthrown in a coup led by officers including Colonel Joe Garba. He was in another country when he stopped being Head of State. Consider what a man in that position usually does. Plots a return. Sulks in exile. Writes bitter memoirs. Buys property. Gowon went to England and enrolled at the University of Warwick, as a student. First as an undergraduate in politics. Then as a doctoral student. And in February 1984, the University of Warwick awarded him a PhD for a thesis titled The Economic Community of West African States: a study in political and economic integration. His supervisor was Ian Campbell. That thesis is in the Warwick Research Archive Portal. You can download it and read it. A former Head of State of Nigeria, sitting in seminars, submitting chapters, being corrected by a supervisor, and being examined like any other candidate. And in 1996, during the Abacha years, he founded Nigeria Prays, a national prayer initiative he has continued to lead. He is alive today. He turned 91 in October 2025.
24.challenge: Learn something this month that puts you back at the bottom of a ladder, deliberately. A language. An instrument. A skill your children already have. Something where you are visibly, obviously a beginner and somebody younger than you is better at it. That experience is a spiritual discipline. Book it this week.
24.prayer: Lord, teach me humility especially in the moments I have power, not only in the moments I lack it. And never let my title persuade me I have finished learning. Amen.

quiz.q: Where did Yakubu Gowon study after he was overthrown?
When was Gowon's PhD awarded?
In what year did Gowon found Nigeria Prays?

25.title: We Fixed the Tax. We Never Fixed the Dollar.

scripture.text: let the wise listen and add to their learning, and let the discerning get guidance.

25.truth: Even the wise must keep listening, because the real danger is a confident wrong diagnosis.
25.hook: In August 1983, the World Bank published a report on Nigeria that said, in effect: the oil money is not coming back to the level you are planning around, and you must change the structure of this economy now. Four months later there was a coup. The report is still online.

points.title: Truth One: Even the wise must keep learning, and the danger is not ignorance, it is the wrong diagnosis confidently held.
points.body: Proverbs 1:5 is remarkable because of who it is addressed to. Let the wise listen and add to their learning. Not the fool. The wise. The people who already know things. Because the most dangerous person in a crisis is not the one who knows nothing. It is the one who knows a lot, has a confident theory, and stops listening to the people telling him his theory is wrong. That is a leadership warning, and it is a personal one. Where in your life do you have a confident diagnosis that you have never allowed anybody to challenge? About your marriage. About your finances. About your child. About why that relationship failed.

points.title: Truth Two: Understanding is available to anyone willing to let the word unfold.
points.body: Psalm 119:130 is one of the kindest verses in the Bible: The unfolding of your words gives light; it gives understanding to the simple. To the simple. Not to the expert. Not to the economist. God's word gives understanding to the person who has no credentials at all, provided they let it unfold, which is a slow word, a patient word. So humility here is not I know nothing. It is: I will keep going back to the source, and I will let it correct me, however long that takes.

supporting.text: The unfolding of your words gives light; it gives understanding to the simple.

25.illustration: Oil prices softened from the second half of 1981. Nigeria's exports fell from twenty-six billion dollars in 1980 to under eighteen billion in 1981. Real GDP turned negative. The fiscal deficit blew out from 0.5% to 9.3% of GDP in a single year. President Shehu Shagari's government responded, and it responded quickly. In April 1982 it passed the Economic Stabilisation Act: import controls, exchange restrictions, higher tariffs, wage restraint. Import volumes did fall. But GDP kept contracting, minus 0.6% in 1982 and minus 4.9% in 1983. The deficit reached 10.8% of GDP. Inflation hit 39%. On 31 December 1983, the government was overthrown. Now here is the correction to how this story is usually told. It is not true that they did nothing. They acted within months. What failed was the diagnosis. The World Bank report of 15 August 1983 urged something specific and unpopular: devalue the naira, and diversify. It warned that real oil earnings are unlikely to regain their 1980 to 1981 levels. Shagari's government chose administrative controls instead, import licences and exchange restrictions. It did not devalue. That came in 1986, under Babangida's Structural Adjustment Programme, and by then the adjustment was far more brutal than it needed to have been. They did something urgent, and they did the wrong thing, because they rejected the counsel that named the real problem. And has Nigeria learned? In two halves. On government revenue, yes, substantially. Oil fell from around 74% of federally collected revenue in 2010 to about 26% in 2024. The tax base was genuinely fixed. On foreign exchange, no. In the fourth quarter of 2025, crude oil alone was 51% of Nigeria's exports, and petroleum products together were around 83%. Genuinely non-oil exports were under 17%. We fixed the tax base. We never fixed the dollar.
25.challenge: Write down one confident opinion you hold about something important: money, politics, a family situation, your own future. Now go and find the best argument against it. Not a weak one. The strongest one you can find, made by someone who actually knows. You do not have to change your mind. You do have to actually read it.
25.prayer: Lord, give me ears that stay open to correction, even when I feel I have already arrived. Unfold Your word to me and give understanding, even to the simple. Amen.
25.code: We fixed the tax base. We never fixed the dollar.

26.title: The Physicist at Nsukka

scripture.text: and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills

26.truth: Technical skill is a spiritual calling, and excellence travels: do the excellent version of the work where you actually are.
26.hook:
We are going to spend the last four days on excellence. And I want to start somewhere unexpected — not with a Nigerian who made it abroad, but with one who stayed.

She is a professor of physics at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. She studies electric currents in the upper atmosphere. And in 2013 she was named one of the five best women scientists in the world.

points.title: Truth One: Technical skill is a spiritual calling, not a secular fallback.
points.body:
We have a hierarchy in our heads. Pastor at the top. Then missionary. Then perhaps doctor. And somewhere far below, engineer, technician, tailor, mechanic, physicist.

Exodus 31 does not know that hierarchy. God says of a metalworker: “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills.” The same Spirit. For skill.

If you are a craftsperson, a technician, an engineer, a coder, a seamstress, a physicist — your competence is not the thing you do to fund your real calling. It may be the calling. And doing it excellently is worship in the most literal Old Testament sense.

points.title: Truth Two: Excellence travels — including to places that look unpromising.
points.body:
Psalm 119:54 has a lovely phrase: “Your decrees are the theme of my song wherever I lodge.” Wherever he happens to be staying. Not in the temple. Not on a good day. Wherever.

We have been taught to believe world-class work requires world-class conditions — that you must first get out, get funded, get abroad. Professor Okeke’s career says otherwise. Excellence is portable. It goes where you go, including to a Nigerian university with unreliable power and a difficult budget.

That is not a romanticisation of scarcity. Nigerian universities should be far better funded than they are. But do not wait for that. Do the excellent version of the work in front of you, where you actually are.

supporting.text: Your decrees are the theme of my song wherever I lodge.

26.illustration:
First, the Scripture, because most people have never noticed this passage.

In Exodus 31, God is setting up the building of the tabernacle. And the very first person in the entire Bible whom God explicitly says He has filled with His Spirit is not a prophet. Not a priest. Not a king.

He is a craftsman. His name is Bezalel, and he works in gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood.

Now hold that beside a Nigerian physicist.

Professor Francisca Nneka Okeke is a Professor of Physics at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. Her field is geophysics — specifically the daily variation of ion currents in the upper atmosphere, the equatorial electrojet, and what those measurements tell us about climate change.

In 2013 she was awarded the L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science Award as the laureate for Africa and the Arab States — one of five women honoured worldwide that year, one per continent. She was elected a Fellow of the Nigerian Academy of Science in 2011. She was the first woman to head her department, and the first woman Dean of the Faculty of Physical Sciences at Nsukka.

She did not do this at MIT. She did it at Nsukka. In Nigeria. With Nigerian students.
26.challenge:
Take the most technical, ordinary, unglamorous part of your work — the part nobody praises — and do it to a standard nobody asked for. Today.

The books balanced to the naira. The report proofread twice. The joint finished properly on the side nobody will see. That is Bezalel’s standard, and God noticed.
26.prayer: Lord, let me see my craft the way You saw Bezalel’s — as worship, not merely as work. And let me do excellent work here, where You have put me. Amen.

quiz.q: Who is the first person in Exodus 31 that God explicitly says He filled with His Spirit?
Where does Professor Okeke teach physics?
In which year was Professor Okeke awarded the L’Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science Award for Africa and the Arab States?

27.title: I Will Not Accept an Inferior Position

scripture.text: Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters.

27.truth: Your real audience is not the person paying you, and excellence is not a decision made at the deadline but one already made about what you love.
27.hook:
In 1956, Queen Elizabeth the Second sat for a Nigerian sculptor.

He made her look African.

points.title: Truth One: Your real audience is not the person paying you.
points.body:
Colossians 3:23 does two things in one sentence. First, “whatever you do” — it removes every excuse of low stakes. There is no task too small to be covered by this. Second, “as working for the Lord, not for human masters” — it relocates your audience.

That is enormously freeing and slightly terrifying. Freeing, because the client’s opinion is no longer the final word on your work. Terrifying, because now there is no such thing as a job nobody will inspect.

Enwonwu had every commercial reason to give the most powerful woman in the world exactly what she and her court expected. He worked for a different audience.

points.title: Truth Two: What you love more than gold determines what you will not do for gold.
points.body:
Psalm 119:127 — “Because I love your commands more than gold, more than pure gold.”

Every craftsperson faces the same moment. The work is not quite right. Fixing it costs you time, and time is money. And there is a voice that says: nobody will notice.

What you do in that moment is decided in advance by what you love more. If you love the money more, you ship it. If you love the standard more, you fix it. Excellence is not a decision you make at the deadline. It is a decision you already made about what you love.

And note what Enwonwu refused: he refused to be graded on a lower scale because he was African. That is a nation-building act. Every Nigerian who does world-standard work, in Nigeria, without apology, moves the whole country’s reputation half a millimetre.

supporting.text: Because I love your commands more than gold, more than pure gold.

27.illustration:
Ben Enwonwu — Odinigwe Benedict Chukwukadibia Enwonwu — was born in 1917 and is generally regarded as the father of Nigerian modernism. He trained at the Slade School of Fine Art in London, at the Ruskin School at Oxford, and studied anthropology at the University of London.

He was both a sculptor and a painter, and you need both halves to understand him.

Around her 1956 visit to Nigeria, he was commissioned to sculpt the Queen. She sat for him in London, and the bronze was unveiled at a Royal Society of British Artists exhibition in 1957.

And here is the thing. His biographer noted that the sculpture “amalgamates the distinctive features of Queen Elizabeth with the serene expression of Enwonwu’s Head of a Yoruba Girl.” His son put it plainly: “the artist depicted the queen through his African eyes — the work had African features, which was characteristic of his style.”

Think about what that took. The most prestigious commission available to any artist in the British Empire — and he did not flatten his own artistic language to please the sitter.

He said it out loud, too. In a BBC interview in 1958: “I will not accept an inferior position in the art world.”

His work “Anyanwu” — “Eye of the Sun” — stands in the United Nations Art Collection in New York. His “Sango”, made in 1964 for what became NEPA, is one of the most recognisable sculptures in Lagos.

And in 1973 he painted three portraits of an Ife princess, Adetutu Ademiluyi — the “Tutu” paintings. They vanished in 1975. One of them was found in a London flat in 2017, and sold at Bonhams in February 2018 for £1,205,000.

He died in 1994.
27.challenge:
Find something you finished recently that you know is not quite right — and that nobody else has noticed.

Go back and fix it. That is the entire assignment, and it will cost you something, which is the point.
27.prayer: Lord, let my work be good enough to sign my name to — because I am really signing Yours. And let me never accept an inferior standard because of where I am from. Amen.
27.code: I will not accept an inferior position in the art world.

quiz.q: Which Nigerian artist made the bronze of Queen Elizabeth II that she sat for in London?
What did Enwonwu say in a BBC interview in 1958?
options: I will not accept an inferior position in the art world.
I will paint only for kings.

quiz.q: Where was one of the Tutu paintings found in 2017?

28.title: The Craft They Called Merely Local

scripture.text: the Lord delights in those who fear him, who put their hope in his unfailing love.

28.truth: Excellence is not only invention but also restoration, and mastery rightly held turns into praise.
28.hook:
There is a kind of Nigerian cloth that used to be described, politely, as “local.” Meaning: fine for here. Not for out there.

One woman spent fifty years proving that was a category error — and she has trained over three thousand young Nigerians, free, to prove it with her.

points.title: Truth One: Excellence is not only invention. It is also restoration.
points.body:
We tend to think excellence means making something new. Sometimes the harder and more valuable act is refusing to let something already valuable be dismissed as ordinary.

Adire did not need improving. It needed somebody to stand in front of it and say: this is not folk material, this is art, and I will not accept it being graded on a lower scale — the same thing Ben Enwonwu said yesterday, said with cloth instead of bronze.

Look around your own community for what is being dismissed as “merely local.” A language. A food. A craft. A form of music. A way of building. Somebody has to be the one who refuses the downgrade.

points.title: Truth Two: Mastery, rightly held, turns into praise.
points.body:
Psalm 119:171 — “May my lips overflow with praise, for you teach me your decrees.”

The praise is because of the teaching. Learning something deeply and praising God are not two separate activities in this verse; one produces the other.

That is a real experience, and any craftsperson knows it. The moment you understand why the joint holds, why the dye takes, why the equation works — there is a response in you that is closer to worship than to pride. Psalm 147:11 says God “delights” in those who fear Him. Delight, on both sides.

And notice her method: she gave it away. Three thousand people, free. Mastery that ends with you is not mastery; it is a hobby with a reputation. You have not truly mastered something until somebody else can do it because of you.

supporting.text: May my lips overflow with praise, for you teach me your decrees.

28.illustration:
Chief Nike Davies-Okundaye was born in Ogidi, Kogi State, in 1951. She learned weaving from her great-grandmother, and trained in indigo dyeing and adire — the resist-dyed cloth of the Yoruba — in Osogbo. Adire and aso-oke were craft traditions passed from mother to daughter, and treated by the wider world as folk material rather than art.

In 1983 she opened the Nike Centre for Art and Culture in Osogbo. In 1996 she opened an aso-oke weaving centre in Ogidi-Ijumu that employs over 200 women. In 2002 she opened a research centre in Abuja. And in Lekki, Lagos, she built the Nike Art Gallery — five floors, around 8,000 works, one of the largest galleries of its kind in West Africa. Four centres in all.

She has trained more than 3,000 young Nigerians free of charge in traditional crafts, and set them up to make a living from them.

Her work has been held by the Smithsonian since 2012. She sits on a UNESCO committee for Nigerian intangible heritage. Rhodes University gave her an honorary doctorate in 2019. She holds the chieftaincy titles Yeye Oba of Ogidi-Ijumu and Yeye Tasase of Osogbo.

She is alive, and still working.
28.challenge:
Teach one person one thing you are good at. This week. For free.

Not a course. Not a programme. One person, one skill, one sitting. That is how Nike Davies-Okundaye got to three thousand.
28.prayer: Lord, give me eyes to see the value in what others have dismissed, and the excellence to restore it. And let me give away what I know. Amen.
28.code: Mastery that ends with you is not mastery

quiz.q: Where was Chief Nike Davies-Okundaye born?
How many young Nigerians has she trained free of charge?
Which resist-dyed cloth of the Yoruba does she train people in?

29.title: What the World Now Concedes

scripture.text: Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank.

29.truth: Skill is only part of the picture: skill plus direction is nation-building, so be excellent and aim it somewhere worth aiming it.
29.hook:
I am going to say something today, and then I am going to say something else immediately afterwards, and I need you to hear both.

The first thing: the world’s most exacting gatekeepers now grade Nigerian work at the very top of the global scale.

The second thing: I am not holding up the personal lives of the people who did it as an example to you. I will explain why I am saying it that way.

points.title: Truth One: Skilled work does not stay hidden.
points.body:
Proverbs 22:29 is one of the few genuinely predictive proverbs. “Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings.”

It does not say connected. It does not say lucky. It says skilled. And it promises reach — that the work will end up in rooms its maker never imagined.

Nobody making a record in a Lagos bedroom in 2015 was planning on London Stadium. Nobody writing code in a Lagos flat in 2015 was planning on Stripe. They were making the work good. The rooms came to find them.

That does not mean skill is always rewarded. It means skill is the only part of this you control — so pour yourself into the part you control.

points.title: Truth Two: The instrument is neutral. The direction is not.
points.body:
Psalm 119:172 — “May my tongue sing of your word, for all your commands are righteous.”

The tongue is the most ordinary instrument any of us owns. It sings, it sells, it argues, it lies, it praises. The psalmist does not ask for a different instrument. He asks for the direction of the one he already has.

That is the whole tension of today. Nigeria has extraordinary creative power. Power is not the same thing as righteousness. A nation can be world-class and still be building nothing.

So the prayer for our creative generation is not “be less excellent.” It is: be excellent, and aim it somewhere worth aiming it. Skill plus direction is nation-building. Skill without direction is just noise at high volume.

And here is the question I want to leave with anyone young watching this. You are almost certainly going to be more skilled than your parents’ generation, with more reach than they ever had. What will you point it at?

supporting.text: May my tongue sing of your word, for all your commands are righteous.

29.illustration:
Start with the hardest gatekeepers there are — the ones who do not care where you are from and cannot be persuaded by sentiment. Venues. Ticket sales. Streaming counts.

In 2018, a Nigerian artist sold out The O2 Arena in London — the first solo African artist to do it. In January 2019, another one did the same.

On 3 June 2023, a Nigerian artist headlined London Stadium in front of more than sixty thousand people — the first African artist ever to headline a UK stadium. Weeks earlier he had performed at the UEFA Champions League Final kick-off show in Istanbul, to a stadium of over seventy-one thousand. In July 2023 he sold out Citi Field in New York, around forty-one thousand people — the first African artist to sell out an American stadium. In April 2022 he had already headlined Madison Square Garden.

On 11 September 2023, “Calm Down” by Rema became the first track led by an African artist to enter Spotify’s Billions Club — one billion streams. It passed two billion by July 2024 and went seven-times platinum in the United States.

And the Grammys. Burna Boy won Best Global Music Album in 2021. Wizkid won Best Music Video as a featured artist on Beyoncé’s “Brown Skin Girl” the same night. Tems won Best Melodic Rap Performance in 2023, and won the new Best African Music Performance category in 2025.

Now — the second thing I promised.

Some of the leading artists in this movement have public conduct I would not commend to you, and lyrical content I would not play in this room. That is a fact and I am not going to pretend otherwise, because half of you already know it and the other half can find out in ten seconds.

So hear exactly what I am claiming, and nothing more. I am not telling you these are men to imitate. I am telling you what the world now concedes about Nigerian work. Those are two entirely different statements.

And so that the point does not rest on music alone: Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986 — the first African laureate in Literature. Ben Okri won the Booker Prize in 1991. Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala — Harvard, then a PhD from MIT — rose to Managing Director for Operations at the World Bank overseeing an $81 billion portfolio, and has been Director-General of the World Trade Organization since March 2021, the first woman and the first African ever to hold the post. And Paystack, founded in Lagos in 2015 by Shola Akinlade and Ezra Olubi, was acquired by Stripe in October 2020 for over $200 million.

That is the range. Literature. Trade. Technology. Music. “Made in Nigeria” is now a claim about standard, not about origin.
29.challenge:
Take the thing you are best at.

Write down one sentence: “I will point this at ______.” A person. A problem. A community. A wrong.

Keep the sentence. You will need it tomorrow.
29.prayer: Lord, let my pursuit of excellence not be for applause. Make me skilled — and then point me somewhere worth pointing. Amen.

quiz.q: Which Nigerian writer won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986?
Which company acquired Paystack in October 2020?
What did the 2018 O2 Arena sellout mark?
options: The first Nigerian to win a Grammy
The first solo African artist to sell out The O2 Arena
The first African to lead the WTO
The first African to win the Booker Prize

30.title: The Nigeria God Intends

scripture.text:
KJV: Righteousness exalteth a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.
NIV: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin condemns any people.

30.truth: God has promised enough light for the next step, and a nation is exalted by righteousness rather than by what it congratulates itself on.
30.hook:
Thirty days ago I told you that Nigeria’s problem was never a shortage of resources.

I want to tell you now what I think it actually is, and then I want to ask you one question.

points.title: Truth One: This was never theology. It was a job description.
points.body:
Integrity. Discipline. Wisdom. Service. Justice. Perseverance. Humility. Excellence.

Those eight words are not a poster. They are the actual mechanism by which a country either works or does not — and they are exercised in the smallest rooms. A nation is the sum of how its people behave when nobody is checking. That is why we started on Day 1 with the only piece of Nigeria you control.

points.title: Truth Two: The lamp shows the next step. That is all it has ever shown.
points.body:
Psalm 119:105 has walked with us for thirty days, one verse at a time. And notice what it actually promises: “a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.”

Feet. Not horizon. A lamp in the ancient world was a small clay oil lamp — it lit roughly the next step, and no further.

God has not promised to show you the whole of Nigeria’s future. He has never promised that to anybody. He has promised enough light for the next step, and He has promised it every single day for the rest of your life.

Which means the question was never “how do we fix Nigeria.” The question is: what is the next step, and will you take it?

supporting.text: Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.

30.illustration:
Let me put the whole month in one breath.

Dora Akunyili gave back twelve thousand pounds nobody knew about, and that is why she was in the room when Nigerians were dying of fake drugs.

Six young corps members ran to a police station in Giade and did not come out, because they had shown up to do an ordinary job.

A young man in Nnewi sold motorcycle parts carefully for years, and ended up building cars.

Vaccinators walked to every village in Nigeria, over and over, for nearly a quarter of a century, until wild polio was gone from this continent.

Chief Awolowo taxed cocoa farmers and put three hundred thousand extra children into classrooms in one year.

Dr Adadevoh picked up a phone, said no to an ambassador, and died of it — and twenty million Lagosians did not get Ebola.

Tai Solarin, who did not believe in God, built a school for the poor and went to prison rather than flatter a dictator.

Zannah Mustapha put the children of Boko Haram fighters in the same classroom as the children of their victims.

Gani Fawehinmi kept a suitcase packed by his door for forty detentions.

Traders in Aba and Onitsha were handed twenty pounds and rebuilt the largest markets in West Africa.

Lucy Ejike won medals at six Paralympic Games on a third of the budget.

Yakubu Gowon stopped being Head of State and went and sat in a classroom in England until they gave him a doctorate.

Professor Francisca Okeke became one of the best scientists in the world — at Nsukka.

Ben Enwonwu sculpted a queen and made her look African.

Nike Davies-Okundaye trained three thousand young Nigerians for free in a craft the world called “merely local.”

Not one of those was a perfect person in a perfect country. Every single one was an imperfect person choosing, in an unfair situation, to build rightly anyway.

That is the whole curriculum. There is nothing else.
30.challenge:
On Day 1, I asked you to write down one thing in your hand that Nigeria would be better off if you did with excellence.

Go and find it.

Now three questions, and I want honest answers, not impressive ones:

1. Which of the eight values is your weakest? Not your favourite. Your weakest. Name it out loud.
2. What is one concrete thing you will do about it, starting tomorrow? Not a resolution. A thing with a day and a time.
3. Who will you tell, so that they can ask you? Day 6 taught us — taken, and confirmed.

And if God asked you today, “What did you build for My Nigeria this month?” — what would your honest answer be?
30.prayer: Lord, thirty days ago You reminded us that except You build the house, we labour in vain. We have walked through Akunyili’s integrity and Adadevoh’s courage, Awolowo’s foresight and Mustapha’s mercy, Fawehinmi’s stubbornness and Ejike’s endurance, Gowon’s humility and Okeke’s excellence. In every one of them we saw not a perfect nation, but an imperfect people choosing, again and again, to build rightly in spite of everything working against them. Make us that kind of people. Not the Nigeria of our complaints — the Nigeria You intend. Righteous enough to be exalted, not condemned. And where we are scattered across other nations, let us build those nations rightly too. Let this not end as thirty days of teaching. Let it begin as a lifetime of building. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
30.code: Enough light for the next step

quiz.q: Which Hebrew word lies behind “reproach” in Proverbs 14:34, according to this day’s teaching?
Which Psalm 119 verse is the lamp verse for this day?
According to the lamp image, how far does a lamp in the ancient world light?
options: The next step, and no further
